title: Family Law Intake Form: What to Ask and Why | CaseAuthority
meta: A family law intake form guide for divorce lawyers: what to ask, conflict checks, safety questions, online forms, privacy and turning consultations into clients.
h1: Family Law Intake Form: What to Ask, What to Avoid and How It Wins Clients
lead: Most family law firms spend real money and effort getting people to call or fill in a form. Then the first thing a nervous person meets is a long, cold questionnaire, or a rushed phone call that misses the one detail that mattered. Your family law intake form sits right at the point where a lead becomes a consultation, and a consultation becomes a retained client. This guide is for divorce and family law attorneys and firm owners who want an intake process that is quick for the client, safe for people in difficult situations and useful for the lawyer: what a good form asks, what it should not ask yet, how to handle conflict checks and safety, how online forms fit in, and how to tell whether your intake is helping or hurting your numbers.
quick_answer: A family law intake form is the set of questions a firm uses to collect basic information from a potential client before or during the first consultation. A good form asks for contact details and safe ways to reach the person, the names of the other party and any children for a conflict check, the type of matter and key dates, any urgent issues such as safety concerns or upcoming court dates, and a short description in their own words. Keep the first form short, save detailed financial questions for after you are hired, ask for a safe phone number and email, and run a conflict check before the person shares sensitive details. Then follow up quickly, because many people contact more than one firm.
takeaways: Intake Is Where Clients Are Won.
A slow or cold first contact can lose a client you already paid to attract.
Ask what you need for the consultation now. Save the full financial picture for after you are hired.
Get the other party’s name before the person tells you their story.
Ask How to Contact Them Safely.
A safe phone number, a safe email and whether it is okay to leave a message.
Safety concerns, court dates and moves with children need a fast human reply.
Track form starts, completions, consultations and retainers by source.

sections.h2: What Is a Family Law Intake Form?
sections.answer: It is the first set of questions a potential client answers, by phone, online or in the office, so the firm can check for conflicts, understand the matter and prepare for a consultation.
paras: Every family law firm has some form of intake, even if it is just a receptionist writing notes on a pad. A family law intake form turns that into a consistent set of questions so nothing important is missed and every person gets the same quality of first contact.

Some firms use one short form for the first contact and a longer client questionnaire after the person hires the firm. Others use a single form for everything. For most firms, splitting it in two works better, because a frightened person deciding whether to call a lawyer is unlikely to finish a 12 page document about their finances.

Intake also shapes how people feel about your firm. The tone of the questions, how long it takes and how quickly someone gets back to them all tell a potential client what working with you will be like. Our guide to [[a:blog/divorce-leads|divorce leads]] covers how people find you before they ever reach the form.

sections.h2: Why Does Intake Matter So Much in Divorce and Family Law?
sections.answer: Because people often contact several firms, many are anxious or unsure, and the firm that responds clearly and kindly first usually wins the consultation.
paras: Divorce and custody decisions are personal and often painful. People may take weeks or months before reaching out, and when they do, they are often reaching out to more than one firm. A fast, warm and clear first response is one of the biggest advantages a family law firm can have.

Intake is also where a lot of marketing money is quietly lost. A firm might invest in its website, Google Business Profile and ads, then let web forms sit for a day, send a generic email or ask so many questions that people give up. Improving intake often brings in more retained clients without spending more on marketing.

Finally, intake protects the firm. A good process catches conflicts of interest before sensitive information is shared, flags urgent safety and court issues, and screens out matters the firm does not handle, so attorney time goes to the right consultations.

sections.h2: What Should a Family Law Intake Form Ask?
sections.answer: Contact and safe contact details, names for the conflict check, the type of matter, children, key dates, urgent issues and a short description in the person’s own words.
paras: The first form should collect what you need to decide whether you can help, to run a conflict check and to prepare for a useful consultation. Anything beyond that can wait until the person has met you and decided to hire you.

Keep the language plain and the questions short. Use drop-down choices where you can, such as the type of matter, and leave one open box for the person to describe what is happening in their own words. That open box often tells you more than any other question.
list: Full name and the best way to reach them, including a safe phone number and email
Whether it is safe to leave a voicemail, send texts or email
Full name of the other party, and any former names, for the conflict check
Type of matter, such as divorce, custody, child support, modification or adoption
Whether there are children, and their ages
County and state where they and the other party live
Whether a case has already been filed, and any upcoming court dates
Whether there are any safety concerns for them or their children
How they heard about the firm
A short description of what is going on and what they hope to achieve

sections.h2: What Should You Not Ask on the First Intake Form?
sections.answer: Detailed financial information, long histories and anything that would be risky to share before a conflict check or a confirmed relationship with your firm.
paras: It is tempting to gather everything at once to save time later. In practice, long first forms reduce completion and can create problems. A person who has not yet hired you should not be asked to list every account, debt and asset, or to upload tax returns, before you even know whether you can take the matter.

Avoid asking for detailed facts about the other party or the relationship until after the conflict check. If the other party has already spoken to your firm, or is a current client, you may not be able to represent this person, and receiving their detailed story can create a problem for your firm.
Leave out questions that sound like judgment. Questions such as who is at fault or why the marriage failed can feel hostile to someone in distress. You will learn what you need in the consultation.

sections.h2: How Do Conflict Checks Fit Into Family Law Intake?
sections.answer: Collect the names of the other party and key people first, and run the conflict check before the person shares their detailed story.
paras: Conflicts are a real risk in family law because both spouses or parents may contact firms in the same area, sometimes on the same day. Attorneys must take care to check for potential conflicts before accepting someone as a client, and in family law that starts at intake.

Design your form so the names come first: the person contacting you, the other party, any former names and, where relevant, new partners. Your team can then check those names against your records before the consultation and before you ask for the full story.

Tell people why you need the names. A short line such as we ask for the other person’s name so we can make sure we are free to help you makes the question feel reasonable, and most people appreciate the care.

Keep the rules in mind for people you do not end up representing. Information shared during intake can still create duties for the firm, which is another reason to keep the first form short and the facts limited until you know you can help.

sections.h2: How Should Intake Handle Safety and Domestic Violence Concerns?
sections.answer: Ask about safety in a simple, direct way, ask how to contact the person safely, and have a clear plan for urgent situations.
paras: Some people contacting a family law firm are in danger. Their partner may read their texts, check their email or share their phone. A form or a follow up call that does not take this into account can put them at risk.

Ask early how it is safe to reach them and whether you can leave a voicemail, send a text or email. Ask a simple question such as do you have any concerns about your safety or your children’s safety right now, and make sure someone reviews that answer quickly.

Have a plan for urgent answers. That might mean a same day call from an attorney, information about emergency protective orders in your state, and sharing the National Domestic Violence Hotline, which offers support by phone, text and online chat. Your team should know exactly what to do when a form shows a safety concern.
Make your online form discreet. Avoid sending automatic confirmation emails with subject lines that mention divorce or abuse, and do not show sensitive answers on screens in a busy reception area.

sections.h2: Should Family Law Firms Use Online Intake Forms?
sections.answer: Yes, for many people an online form is easier than a phone call, but it must be short, mobile friendly, secure and followed up fast.
paras: Many people looking into divorce prefer to start privately. They may research late at night or on a lunch break and would rather fill in a form than make a call where someone might overhear them. An online intake form gives them an easy first step.

Most of those people will be on a phone, so test your form on one. Large buttons, short fields, clear labels and a progress bar if it has more than one step all help. If the form takes more than a few minutes, it is probably too long.

Use a secure form tool and limit who can see the answers. Intake answers often contain highly sensitive information, so they should not land in a shared inbox that the whole office can read, and the form should send data over a secure connection.

Speed matters more online than on the phone. Someone who fills in a form at 10pm and hears nothing until the next afternoon may already have booked with another firm. An automatic, discreet message that confirms you received their request and says when you will be in touch helps, but it does not replace a fast human reply.

sections.h2: How Should the First Phone Intake Call Go?
sections.answer: Warm, calm and organized: confirm safe contact details, collect names for the conflict check, understand the basics and book a consultation.
paras: Many family law clients still prefer to call. The person answering is often the first human voice they hear from your firm, so training matters. A calm, kind tone and a clear structure do more for conversion than any script.

Start by confirming that it is a good time to talk and that they can speak safely. Then collect names for the conflict check, the type of matter and any urgent issues. Explain clearly what the next step is, such as a consultation with an attorney, what it involves and how to prepare.

Be careful about who is on the call. If a friend, parent or new partner is listening, the confidentiality of the conversation may be put at risk if a third party is present during a privileged communication, unless that person is essential. Many firms ask to speak with the potential client alone for this reason, and explain why.

sections.h2: What Happens After the Intake Form Is Submitted?
sections.answer: Review it quickly, run the conflict check, reply within hours, and send clear information about the consultation.
paras: A good intake process has clear steps and clear owners. Someone reviews new forms during set times each day, flags urgent issues for an attorney right away, runs the conflict check and contacts the person using the method they said was safe.

Confirm the consultation in writing, using their safe contact details, with the date, time, location or video link, what to bring and what it costs if there is a fee. A short checklist of documents to gather helps people arrive prepared and shows them that your firm is organized.

Explain what happens next. Many people do not know how a family law case begins, what a retainer is or how fees work. Lawyers generally need to explain the scope of the work and the basis of the fee, preferably in writing, so it helps to prepare a plain summary of how your fees work before the consultation.

sections.h2: How Does Intake Turn Consultations Into Retained Clients?
sections.answer: By making the consultation easy to book and attend, following up kindly with people who are still deciding, and removing confusion about fees and next steps.
paras: Not everyone who has a consultation hires a lawyer on the spot. Divorce is a big decision, and many people need time. A short, respectful follow up a few days after the consultation, with a summary of next steps and an easy way to ask questions, often brings people back when they are ready.
Make the retainer process simple. Clear fee agreements, online signing and easy payment options remove small barriers that can stall a decision for weeks.

Keep track of why people did not hire you when you can. Common reasons include cost, timing, a decision to try to reconcile or choosing another firm. Patterns in those reasons can show you where to improve. Our guide to [[a:blog/email-marketing-for-divorce-lawyers|email marketing for divorce lawyers]] covers how to stay in touch with people who are still deciding.

sections.h2: What Are Common Family Law Intake Mistakes?
sections.answer: Slow replies, forms that are too long, missing conflict checks, unsafe contact methods and no tracking of where clients came from.
paras: Slow follow up is the most common problem. Firms that respond within an hour or two during business hours, and first thing the next morning for overnight forms, usually book more consultations than firms that reply when someone has time.
Long first forms come next. Every extra question gives a nervous person another reason to stop. Cut the first form to what you need for the conflict check and the consultation.

Other common mistakes include sending sensitive messages to an email address the other party may read, leaving voicemails without asking whether it is safe, and taking detailed stories before checking conflicts. These are easy to fix with a clear process and a little training.
Finally, many firms do not track the source of each new client. Without that, it is hard to know whether your website, Google profile, referrals or ads are bringing in the clients you want.

sections.h2: How Do You Measure Whether Your Intake Process Is Working?
sections.answer: Track each step: form starts, completed forms, calls answered, consultations booked, consultations held and retainers signed, by source.
paras: Start with a simple monthly report. How many people started your online form and how many finished it? How many calls came in, and how many were answered by a person? How many consultations were booked and held, and how many became retained clients?

Look at the gaps between steps. A big drop between form starts and completions usually means the form is too long or hard to use on a phone. A big drop between booked and held consultations may mean reminders are missing or the process feels uncertain. A drop between consultations and retainers often points to fees, follow up or fit.

Break the numbers down by source where you can. If people from Google search finish your form but rarely book, while referrals almost always book, that tells you where to focus. Our guide to [[a:local-seo-for-divorce-lawyers|local SEO for divorce lawyers]] covers how to bring in more of the right people at the top.

sections.h2: A Note on Rules and Examples
sections.answer: Ethics and privacy rules vary by state, and the examples here are general.
paras: This article gives general information, not legal or ethics advice. Rules about prospective clients, conflicts, confidentiality, fees and record keeping vary by state, and so do protective order procedures. Check your state bar’s rules and speak to an ethics counsel if you are unsure how they apply to your intake process.

faq.q: What Is a Family Law Intake Form?
faq.a: It is the set of questions a family law firm uses to collect basic information from a potential client, such as contact details, the other party’s name for a conflict check, the type of matter, children, key dates and urgent issues, before or during the first consultation.

faq.q: What Questions Should Be on a Divorce Intake Form?
faq.a: Safe contact details, the names of both parties, the type of matter, whether there are children and their ages, the county, whether a case has been filed, any upcoming court dates, any safety concerns and a short description in the person’s own words.

faq.q: Should a Family Law Intake Form Ask About Finances?
faq.a: Usually not on the first form. Detailed financial questions are better saved for a client questionnaire after the person hires the firm. A short first form gets more completions and avoids collecting sensitive details too early.

faq.q: Why Do Family Law Firms Ask for the Other Party’s Name?
faq.a: To check for conflicts of interest. If the other party has already contacted the firm or is a client, the firm may not be able to help. Checking names first protects both the potential client and the firm.

faq.q: Is an Online Intake Form Safe for Divorce Clients?
faq.a: It can be, if it uses a secure form tool, limits who can see the answers, asks how to contact the person safely and avoids revealing confirmation emails. Fast, discreet follow up is just as important as the form itself.

faq.q: How Quickly Should a Family Law Firm Respond to an Intake Form?
faq.a: As quickly as possible, ideally within an hour or two during business hours and first thing the next morning for overnight forms. Many people contact more than one firm, and the first clear, kind reply often wins the consultation.
